newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German M3 slows faster than expected in Nov.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German M3 slows faster than expected in Nov.

text.p: The Bundesbank said on Wednesday that growth in its main monetary policy indicator, M3 money supply, slowed markedly in November, surprising economists who had expected only a moderate ease in the rate.
The central bank said in a statement that that German M3 money supply growth slowed to an annualised rate of 8.0 percent in November after 8.4 percent in October.
Economists welcomed the better-than-expected figure but said it did not change their views that the central bank is unlikely to make any change in its monetary policy near-term.

Gertrude Traud of Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt said in an initial reaction to the data, "The figure is remarkably below expectations. We had foreseen growth of 8.2 percent. I haven't seen the details yet but I would expect that the so-called Telekom effect was less than expected."

Traud was refering to the sale of Deutsche Telekom shares in November. The Bundesbank had warned this was likely to boost M3 as investors parked money in cash or accessible acounts in anticipation of the flotation, which was Europe's largest.

Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at Industrial Bank of Japan in London told Reuters Financial Television, "The figure is a little bit better than expected. It gives good grounds to hope that the January figure will be a very low rate."

Hans-Juergen Metzler, economist at Deutsche Bank Research, told Reuters Financial Television, "It's a good number. We had been expecting a higher rate. It is slightly above target, but one should not be overly concerned about the target."
The Bundesbank set a target of four to seven percent for M3 growth in 1996 and is due to set its 1997 target on Thursday.
Economists expect it to pitch the 1997 goal at an unchanged or slightly lower level. The target compares growth with the average level of M3 in the final quarter of the previous year.
Some also believe the central bank will set a two-year target this time, paving the way for the transfer of monetary policy power to the European Central Bank at the end of 1998.
Edmonds at IBJ said that the good November data meant that the Bundesbank might now be able to afford to set a more ambitious target for next year.
"That will encourage the Bundesbank to set a tougher M3 target for 1997. I would expect a target of four to six percent rather than the current four to seven percent," he said.
In its statement, the central bank said that M3 grew only moderately on average during November and eased over the course of the month.
"After the strong rise in money stock in October, monetary development in November slowed perceptibly," the central bank said in a statement.
The central bank said a clear rise in monetary capital formation -- the transfer of funds out of M3 into longer-term forms of investment -- had helped to dampen M3 growth.
Bank lending to doemstic non-banks remained buoyant but public sector lending slowed slightly while private sector lending grew.
Among savings components, only savings accounts grew in the period while other components eased.
"Even sight deposits, which rose unexpectedly fast in the previous month due to the acquisition of Telekom shares, were scaled back considerably," the Bundesbank said.
